analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to pay 50 cents per hour into workers' retirement accounts, funded by higher taxes on top earners and corporations.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2019 with 3 Democratic cosponsors, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require employers with 10 or more full-time-equivalent workers to contribute at least 50 cents for every hour an employee works into a retirement plan, rising to 60 cents after two years. Workers would be automatically enrolled in portable 'UP' retirement accounts, contributing 4% of wages unless they opt out, with contributions automatically rising to 10% unless they opt out, plus a small savings account of up to $2,500 they could tap for emergencies like a big medical bill or a home down payment. Small employers would get tax credits to cover part of the cost. To pay for it, the bill would raise the top individual income tax rate from 37% to 39.6% and the corporate rate from 21% to 23%.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at employers with 10 or more employees who currently have no workplace retirement plan. The bill's own findings cite that about 3 in 10 private-sector workers lack access to any workplace plan, and that over half of households age 55 and older have no retirement savings in a defined contribution plan or IRA.

how_it_helps.text: Requires employers with 10 or more full-time-equivalent employees to contribute at least 50 cents per hour worked into a qualified pension plan for each employee, rising to 60 cents per hour after two years and indexed upward over time [S2][S3].

Auto-enrolls employees in portable UP retirement accounts at 4% of wages (with an opt-out), with contributions auto-escalating by half a point a year up to 10% (opt-out), and employer matching up to 10% of wages [S2][S3].

Creates UP savings accounts of up to $2,500 (growing with wages) that workers can withdraw from for nonroutine needs like a large medical bill or a home down payment, with no withdrawal penalty and no repayment requirement [S3].

Gives small employers a tax credit covering 50% of required contributions for their first 15 employees and 25% for the next 15, and more than quadruples the small-employer plan startup credit from $500 to $2,000 [S3].
Gives a 50% tax credit on retirement contributions to people whose employer offers no plan or who are not employed [S3].

The default investment option must minimize fees, be diversified, and reduce risk as the worker approaches retirement, and no single private investment firm may administer more than $500 billion of account assets [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 10 or more full-time-equivalent employees owe the new per-hour contribution for every worker not already in a defined benefit pension plan, plus payroll costs of administration. Top-bracket individual taxpayers pay 2.6 points more (37% to 39.6%) and corporations pay 2 points more (21% to 23%) to cover the credits. Workers also have take-home pay reduced by the default 4% auto-enrolled contribution unless they opt out.

drawbacks.text: The mandate raises labor costs for employers with 10 or more employees; even with the credit offsetting half the required contribution for the first 15 workers, employers bear the full cost for everyone beyond their first 30 employees [S3].

Workers are auto-enrolled at 4% of wages with automatic escalation to 10% unless they affirmatively opt out, which reduces take-home pay for employees living paycheck to paycheck who do not opt out [S3].
The bill pays for its credits by raising the top individual rate to 39.6% and the corporate rate to 23%, which its opponents would characterize as a tax increase on job creators and investors [S3].

The bill contains drafting defects: the new individual saver credit is keyed to a 'base amount' referencing a section of the bill (802(a)(3)(i)) that does not define any contribution amount, leaving the credit's size undefined as introduced [S3].

The new federal board must contract with private investment firms to administer the accounts, so fees for recordkeeping and investment management would come out of workers' returns, even though the default options are required to minimize fees [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and large: a mandatory employer contribution plus auto-enrollment would give retirement savings to the roughly 30% of private-sector workers the bill says have no workplace plan, and the emergency-savings feature addresses a genuine gap in how 401(k)-style accounts work. The costs are also real: a new per-hour payroll obligation on covered employers, reduced take-home pay for auto-enrolled workers who don't opt out, and higher tax rates on top earners and corporations to fund the small-employer credits. The design has notable flaws for a bill of this ambition — the individual credit is keyed to an amount the text never defines — so it would likely have needed substantial reworking in committee even if it had moved.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — and it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Chris Coons introduced the bill on April 4, 2019, for himself and Sen. Amy Klobuchar [S1][S3].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance [S5].
The action history shows no further action of any kind — no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote — through the end of the 116th Congress [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers with 10 or more employees are better off because the per-hour contribution requirement never became law, and top-bracket individual taxpayers and corporations are better off keeping the 37% and 21% rates. Workers without a workplace retirement plan are no better off than before; a later Congress would take up similar ideas.

for.name: Sen. Chris Coons
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate Finance Committee; the bill carried his name alone in the introduction.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's co-introducer when it was introduced.

for.name: Three Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican (Chuck Grassley)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, a markup, or a vote on it during the two years remaining in the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat and no Republican signed on, but the bill never got a hearing or vote, so no roll call exists showing where either party's members actually stood.

industries.note: They would owe at least 50 cents per hour worked for every employee not already covered by a defined benefit pension plan, a direct new labor cost that is the workers' benefit. Small employers get a partial tax credit for their first 30 employees only.

industries.industry: Private investment and retirement-plan administration firms
industries.note: The bill makes private investment firms the permanent administrators of a new universal savings system, with a cap of $500 billion in assets per firm. Their fees would come out of workers' returns, though default investment options must minimize fees.
They would pay for the small-employer credits through the higher 39.6% individual and 23% corporate rates; their savings under the bill's design fund the benefit workers receive.

industries.industry: Small employers (under 10 employees) and small-plan service providers
industries.note: Employers below the 10-employee threshold are exempt from the mandate, and the startup-credit expansion (from $500 to $2,000, with eligibility extended) plus the new contribution credit subsidize small employers and SIMPLE-IRA and state-based plan providers.
